docs.text: 🎾 Topic Deep Dive — Lob and Overhead ¶ *The Vertical Game ¶ Assumptions - Skill level: 3.5 recreational (USTA > - Depth: standard — simple cues, clear drills, no frame-by-frame physics - Language: EN - Voice: friendly master coach, honest about difficulty, focused on what you can copy this month - The big ideas: (1) Tennis is a vertical game as much as horizontal. (2) The lob buys you time; the overhead cashes the time in. (3) At 50+, the lob is your insurance policy; the overhead is your reward. - Rational default for 3.5+: Defensive slice lob + Sane (controlled) overhead.** Offensive topspin lob and full-power smash are labelled "reference" and "for the brave." 📖 Table of Contents ¶ The Big Idea — The Vertical Game The Lob — Defensive + Offensive (The Insurance Policy) The Overhead — The Sane Smash (The 50+ Reward) The Specialty Shots — Lob Volley + Counter-Overhead Drills, Cues, Warnings, 50+ Check & Printable Cheat Sheet Chapter 1 — The Big Idea: The Vertical Game ¶ 🇺🇸 English Watch any point at your club that ends in 4 shots or fewer. Watch the rally. Watch the geometry. The shot that ENDS the point is almost never a flat cross-court groundstroke. It's almost always a shot that went up or down — a high lob that the opponent can't reach, or a smash that the opponent can only block. Recreational tennis is dominated by the horizontal game — cross-court, down-the-line, angled. But the vertical game — high balls, lobs, smashes — is what decides points, especially when opponents are skilled enough to retrieve everything from side to side. This deep dive is about the vertical game. Two shots: the lob (you hit it up) and the overhead (they hit it up, you put it down). 🧠 Mental model Imagine a chess board. Horizontal moves (left-right) gain space. Vertical moves (forward-back, up-down) change the rules of the game . A lob doesn't just put the ball in the corner — it tells the opponent: you must hit the next shot from below your shoelaces, with your head looking up, while standing still or moving backward. That's a fundamentally different problem from "return a flat ball while balanced at net." That's why lobs and overheads decide points. The "Ladder of 4 Situations" — When to Use Vertical Tennis ¶ Most 3.5 players think of the lob and the overhead as separate strokes. They're not — they're paired answers to the same problem : the ball is high (or the opponent is at the net). Here is the entire decision tree: Situation English The shot Why it works 1. You are at the baseline, opponent is at the net, you are under pressure 🇺🇸 Defensive Lob (slice) The ball goes over their head, deep, into the corner. You buy time to recover. 2. You are at the baseline, opponent is at the baseline, you want to attack 🇺🇸 Offensive Lob (topspin) Topspin lob dips back down inside the court. Opponent has to hit a high ball on the run. 3. Opponent hits a high ball to you (a lob, a moonball, a floater) 🇺🇸 **Overhead ** 🇻🇳 **Overhead ** The ball is already in the air. You finish the point. 4. You are at the net, opponent lobs over you 🇻🇳 Lob Volley (nếu không kịp lùi) The lob volley is your emergency parachute. The overhead is your finishing move. ⚠️ The 3.5 trap Most 3.5 players only ever practice Situation 4's lob volley (defensive) and never practice Situation 1 (defensive lob) or Situation 3 (overhead). They panic on every high ball. They hit a weak "moon" lob when they should be hitting a deep slice lob. They flail at overheads. The whole point of this deep dive: practice all 4 situations, starting with the defensive lob and the controlled overhead.** The Vertical Game in Tai Chi ¶ Principle Vietnamese What it means for lobs and overheads Hư - Thực A lob creates hư (emptiness) behind the opponent. An overhead exploits a real thực (substantial) high ball. Together they form the hư-thực cycle: you create space, then you fill it. Bước cung The overhead stance is a literal bow stance — front foot forward, back foot anchored, weight loaded. Same as tai chi's Cung Bộ . Lực tĩnh A good lob is quiet power — minimum racket speed, maximum arc. A good overhead is the same — minimum effort, maximum placement. Neither shot is a "swing hard" shot. Cuộn lại The defensive lob is a Lã Kình move — you yield to your opponent's pressure and redirect it upward and over their head. 🩺 The 50+ framing The lob and the overhead are the two most longevity-friendly shots in tennis. The lob is a slow, low-impact motion (no shoulder load, no violent rotation). The overhead uses gravity as the engine — you don't need to swing hard; you just need to point the racket at the ball. Both shots save your joints compared to a baseline rally.** That's why we'll lead with them in this deep dive. Chapter 2 — The Lob: Defensive + Offensive (The Insurance Policy) ¶ 🇺🇸 English The lob is the most under-appreciated shot in 3.5 tennis. Not because it's flashy — because it works . A 50+ player who can hit a deep, arcing defensive lob to the opponent's weaker corner will save more points than a 50+ player who can hit a 70 mph forehand. The lob is slow on your body, devastating on theirs, and it asks nothing of your shoulder. The Two Lobs — Pick Yours (Lead with the Defensive Slice) ¶ |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Defensive Slice Lob | 🇻🇳 High arc, deep, slow, underspin | 🇺🇸 When you're under pressure at the baseline, opponent is at the net | 🇻🇳 Continental (the volley grip) | 🇺🇸 A "rainbow" — high enough to clear the opponent's reach, deep enough to land near the baseline | | Offensive Topspin Lob | 🇻🇳 Faster, lower, dipping topspin | 🇺🇸 When you want to attack from the baseline against a baseline opponent who is hitting weak balls | 🇻🇳 Same as groundstroke (Semi-W or Eastern) | 🇺🇳 Lower arc, lands inside the court, kicks UP after the bounce | 🧠 Which is for 3.5? Lead with the defensive slice lob. The offensive topspin lob is beautiful when Federer does it, but at 3.5 it requires: (1) reading the opponent's depth, (2) loading the legs, (3) generating real racket head speed, (4) hitting a precise margin. Get all four right or the ball lands in the bottom of the net. The defensive slice lob asks: (1) Continental grip, (2) high finish, (3) aim deep. That's it.** The defensive lob is your insurance policy. The offensive lob is "for the brave." Defensive Slice Lob — The Default ¶ 🎯 Part 1 — The Setup (Grip + Stance + Backswing) ¶ 🇺🇸 English Grip: Continental. The same V-to-bevel-2 grip you use for the volley. This is the single most important decision. Eastern or Semi-Western will force the face open at contact, and the lob will fly long. Stance: open or semi-open. Stand with the front foot already pointed slightly toward the sideline (not straight at the net). This is different from your groundstroke stance. The open stance lets the chest rotate upward instead of "into" the ball. Backswing: short and HIGH. The racket goes back like a tennis serve's takeback — racket head UP, elbow bent, like you're about to scratch your back with the racket. The high backswing is what gives the lob its arc. A low backswing = a flat shot = an overhead for your opponent. 💡 The "scratch your back" cue Stand in your ready position. Lift the racket as if to scratch the middle of your back. That's the lob backswing. The higher the backswing, the higher the arc.** This is a good thing. Most 3.5 players hit a "moon" lob because they keep the backswing low and try to lift with the wrist. Don't lift with the wrist. Lift with the backswing. 🎯 Part 2 — The Contact (The "Up and Over" Feeling) ¶ 🇺🇸 English Contact point: in front of the body, slightly higher than a normal groundstroke contact. For a forehand lob, the ball should be caught at about chest-to-shoulder height. For a backhand lob, slightly lower (waist-to-chest). Racket face: slightly OPEN. The Continental grip does this naturally. The face should look like it's "holding water" — a slight cup. A flat face = a flat shot = a smash for the opponent. Swing path: low-to-high, brushing UP the back of the ball. The racket path is more vertical than a normal groundstroke. Imagine drawing a vertical line from knee to head — that's your swing path. The "shoulder shrug" cue: as you make contact, shrug the hitting shoulder UP toward your ear. This adds 6-12 inches of height to the arc — and it doesn't strain the shoulder because the motion is gentle , not violent. 🎯 The mirror check Stand in your open stance. Do the "scratch your back" backswing. Now imagine the ball is at chest height, in front of you. Sweep the racket from low (knee) to high (head), face slightly open, shoulder shrug at the top. Your racket should end ABOVE your head, almost like a mini-serve.** That's the lob. Practice the air swing 10 times. Then add a ball. 🎯 Part 3 — The Aim and Depth (Where to Land It) ¶ 🇺🇸 English Aim: deep, into the corner. The lob should land within 2-3 feet of the baseline , near the deuce or ad sideline. A lob that lands in the middle of the service box gives your opponent an easy overhead. A lob that lands in the corner forces them to either (a) run 20+ feet to retrieve it, or (b) hit a desperate, off-balance overhead. The "moon vs. rainbow" line: the minimum arc is when the ball clears the opponent's reach by about 2 feet. The maximum useful arc is when the ball JUST clears the net by 3-4 feet. Anything higher than that wastes energy and gives the opponent time to set up. Aim for the weaker side: if you know your opponent's backhand overhead is shaky, lob to their backhand. The lob's purpose is not just to clear them — it's to make them hit a difficult overhead. 🧠 The "Pass the test" mental model Before you hit the lob, ask: will this ball clear the highest part of their reach AND land within 3 feet of the baseline? If the answer to both is yes, hit it. If either is no, either add more arc (lift the shoulder more) or aim for the deeper part of the court. A lob that doesn't pass the test is a free point for the opponent.** Offensive Topspin Lob — The Brave Shot (Reference) ¶ 🇺🇸 English The offensive lob is the inverse of the defensive lob. Same idea (ball goes over the opponent's head), different execution. Grip: same as your groundstroke (Semi-W or Eastern). The face needs to close over the top of the ball to generate topspin. Contact: lower and more aggressive. The ball is hit at about waist height, with a brushing-up motion, brushing the back of the ball from 7 o'clock to 1 o'clock (or 5 to 11 for backhand). The topspin makes the ball dip back down inside the court. Trajectory: lower arc, lands inside. The offensive lob clears the net by only 1-2 feet and lands inside the court. The topspin makes the ball "kick up" after the bounce, which is what bothers the opponent. When to use it: against a baseline opponent who is hitting weak, loopy balls from the back of the court. The offensive lob is a counter-attack. 🇺🇸 English --- The overhead smash is the most under-shot shot in 3.5 tennis. Recreational players see a high ball, panic, run around in circles, and either shank it into the fence or float it back as a moonball. Here's the truth: the overhead is a serve that comes to you. Same grip (Continental), same contact point (racket head above the ball, fully extended), same finish (over the non-dominant shoulder). The only thing different is the ball is in the air instead of being tossed. Once you see the overhead as "a serve that already happened," the panic disappears. You have all the time in the world. You don't need to swing hard. You just need to point the racket at the ball and let gravity help. Why Recreational Players Miss Overheads ¶ 🇺🇸 English Reason 1 — They don't get into position early. The ball is high, the player is at the baseline, the lob keeps rising. The player runs around, looks up, and arrives just as the ball is at its peak. You must be in position BEFORE the ball reaches its peak. That means tracking the lob from the moment it leaves your opponent's racket. Reason 2 — They look up at the sky. The moment you tilt your head back, your body starts to lean back too. The leaning-back posture takes the legs out of the shot — and legs are the engine of the overhead. Keep your head still, eyes on the ball, chin level. Reason 3 — They try to "swing" the overhead like a groundstroke. A groundstroke generates pace by swinging. An overhead generates pace by falling — the racket falls from a high position, gravity does the work. No swing needed. Just point and fall. Reason 4 — They use the wrong grip. Using Eastern or Semi-Western for the overhead puts the racket face too open at contact, and the ball flies long. Continental is mandatory — same as the serve. 🧠 The "serve that already happened" mental model Every overhead is a serve. The opponent just tossed it for you. You have all the time in the world to set up. The ball is in the air, coming down at a comfortable pace. The net is the same height. The court is the same shape. The only difference from your serve: you're not tossing, you're intercepting. Treat the overhead like a serve and your success rate will jump from 30% to 80%.** The Sane Smash — 3.5+ Overhead Framework ¶ 🎯 Part 1 — The Tracking and Stance ¶ 🇺🇸 English Step 1: Side-shuffle to position. The instant your opponent makes contact with the lob, side-shuffle so the ball will land slightly IN FRONT of your lead foot. The ball's "sweet spot" is about 1-2 feet in front of the front foot. Step 2: Turn sideways to the ball. Once in position, rotate your body so the non-dominant shoulder points to the ball. You're now in a serve-ready position — same as the start of a serve. | Step 4: Free arm UP, racket arm LIFTING. Non-dominant hand points at the ball (it tracks it, like a serve toss). Racket arm lifts up, racket head above the head, elbow bent. This is the "trophy position" of the serve. | 💡 The "two-arm" cue At the trophy position of the overhead, your arms should look identical** to the trophy position of your serve. Non-dominant arm pointing at the ball (or just tossed), racket arm bent with head above. If you've ever hit a serve, you already know this position. The overhead is just the next rep. 🎯 Part 2 — The Contact and Finish (The "Fall, Don't Swing") ¶ 🇺🇸 English Contact: at full extension, racket head above the ball. Reach up. The contact point is the highest comfortable point of your reach. The ball is caught between the strings and gravity. Racket face: slightly closed, going down through the ball. The Continental grip naturally puts the face in the right position. The racket path goes down and through the ball — same as a serve. The ball goes down because of (a) the downward racket path, (b) gravity. The "sane smash" cue: instead of "SMASH IT," say "PUT IT DOWN." You're not generating pace — gravity is generating pace. You're just placing the ball in the court. Aim: cross-court OR down the line — both are valid. The cross-court is the safer choice (more net clearance, more margin). The down-the-line is the "winner" choice (shorter distance to the sideline). At 3.5, lead with the cross-court. Finish: over the non-dominant shoulder, racket head pointing down-and-back. Same as a serve. If your finish is over the dominant shoulder or in front of your body, your chest didn't turn. 🧠 The "downward" mental model Watch a pro hit an overhead. The racket head is at the top, the ball is below it, the racket "falls" through the ball. The ball is in the air for less than half a second. You don't have time to swing. You have time to point and let go. The "swing" is just the racket continuing its downward path after the ball has been hit. Less is more.** ⚠️ The 3.5 trap with overheads Recreational players often try to "muscle" the overhead. They grip it tight, swing hard, and the ball flies long or into the net. The Sane Smash is the opposite: grip pressure 3-4/10, swing speed 30% of a forehand, and the ball goes IN because gravity and downward angle do the work.** A controlled 50 mph overhead is a winner at 3.5. A panicked 80 mph overhead is a fault. The Three Overhead Situations ¶ Situation Position of the ball The Sane Smash adjustment 1. Easy high ball (the opponent's lob is short) Ball is at or above net height, falling comfortably Standard smash. Full extension, full Sane Smash. Aim cross-court, place the ball. 2. Behind you (the opponent's lob is deep) Ball is behind your body, above your head Turn and shuffle. Side-shuffle back so the ball is in front of you. Don't try to hit an overhead with the ball behind you — that's a backhand smash, and at 3.5, the only backhand smash worth hitting is a controlled block back. Easier solution: if the lob is too deep, let it bounce. You now have a normal groundstroke. 3. Moving backward (you're running back as the lob drops) Ball is above you, you're still moving Plant, then hit. Stop your feet first, then hit. Hitting on the run is a recipe for error. The Sane Smash is a still shot, not a moving shot. 🩺 The 50+ rule for overheads At 50+, the Sane Smash is your reward for hitting good defensive lobs in your previous points. The ball comes to you, gravity does the work, your shoulder doesn't take a heavy load. The only risk is the head-still cue — your neck doesn't love craning backward. Keep your chin level, eyes tracking the ball, and let the ball come DOWN to you instead of you reaching UP for it. If the lob is so high that you have to crane your neck, let it bounce.** A 3.5-controlled forehand from the baseline is a better shot than a 50+ overstretched overhead. Chapter 4 — The Specialty Shots: Lob Volley + Counter-Overhead ¶ 🇺🇸 English The lob volley and the counter-overhead are the two "specialty" vertical shots that complete your toolkit. Both are situational — you won't use them every point — but when the situation calls for them, they're devastating. Both were introduced in the Volley deep dive (Ch 4). Here we expand them with the 3.5+ decision tree for when to use them. 4A. The Lob Volley — Your Net Emergency Parachute ¶ 🇺🇸 English When: you're at the net, opponent is at the net or approaching, you can't get past them. The lob volley is the "I can't pass you, so I'll go over you" shot. Grip: Continental (same as the defensive lob). Contact: HIGH, at or above shoulder height. The lob volley only works when you catch the ball high. If the ball is at your waist or lower, hit a normal volley or a half-volley — the lob volley from a low contact is a guaranteed net error. Racket face: open, almost vertical. Open the face, lift the ball. The non-dominant hand reaches UP to track the ball (and to balance the shoulders — like the tai chi "Embrace the Moon" posture from the volley deep dive). Aim: deep, into the corner. Same aim as the groundstroke defensive lob. A short lob volley is a smash for the opponent. Recovery: BACK to the net. As soon as the lob volley is in the air, recover to the net. Don't retreat. If the opponent retrieves the lob, you want to be at the net for the next shot. 🇺🇸 English --- When: you're at the net, opponent lobs over you, you have time to set up. The counter-overhead is the "I see your lob, I will put it down" shot. This is the same Sane Smash as Chapter 3 , but from a starting position at the net instead of the baseline. The mechanics are identical. The only difference: you don't have as much time (you're closer to the net, the ball has less distance to travel), so you must start tracking the lob earlier. Step 1 — As soon as the lob leaves the opponent's racket, side-shuffle BACK. Don't stand flat-footed and watch it rise. Side-shuffle back as it rises, get into position BEFORE it peaks. Step 2 — Once in position, turn into the serve-ready stance (same as the baseline overhead). Step 3 — Sane Smash as in Chapter 3. ⚠️ The 3.5 trap with the counter-overhead Many 3.5 players see the lob, panic, and run straight back without turning their body. They arrive at the ball looking up, off-balance, and hit a weak floater. The fix: track the lob, side-shuffle back, then TURN into the serve stance.** The turn is what gives you the same Sane Smash as your serve. The Vertical Game Decision Tree ¶ BALL IS IN THE AIR → What's the situation? ├─ I lobbed it, opponent is running back │ └─ Did they reach it? │ ├─ YES, they hit a defensive ball → RECOVER, hit a normal groundstroke │ └─ NO, it's a winner → CONGRATULATIONS │ ├─ Opponent lobbed, I'm at the baseline │ └─ Can I get in position? │ ├─ YES → SANE SMASH (Ch 3): track, position, turn, fall │ └─ NO (lob too deep, I'm out of position) → LET IT BOUNCE, hit a normal forehand/backhand │ ├─ Opponent lobbed, I'm at the net │ └─ Can I get in position? │ ├─ YES → COUNTER-OVERHEAD (Ch 4B): shuffle back, turn, Sane Smash │ └─ NO (lob is perfect, I'm stuck at net) → LOB VOLLEY (Ch 4A): high contact, deep aim, recover to net │ └─ I'm at the baseline, opponent is at the net, I'm under pressure └─ DEFENSIVE LOB (Ch 2): Continental, high backswing, deep aim 🩺 The 50+ pattern in doubles The vertical game is the best doubles weapon for 50+ players. Why? Doubles opponents at the net are usually 8-10 feet away from you. A defensive lob is the easiest way to neutralize them — they have to hit a high overhead on the move. And your doubles partner can poach the weak reply. The pattern: my partner serves, I hit a deep defensive lob, partner poaches the reply. Three shots, one point.** This is the 50+ doubles cheat code. Chapter 5 — Drills, Cues, Warnings, 50+ Reality Check & Printable Cheat Sheet ¶ 🛠️ The 5 Drills You Can Do This Week ¶ Drill 1 — The "Scratch Your Back" Lob Air Swing (Solo, 2 min/day) ¶ 🇺🇸 English Stand in your open stance, racket in Continental grip. Do the "scratch your back" backswing. Sweep the racket from low to high, face slightly open, shoulder shrugs at the top. Do 20 air swings per day, every day, for 2 weeks. Why this works: the lob backswing is the part 3.5 players skip. They go straight from "ready" to "hit." The backswing IS the shot — without it, the lob has no arc. Drill 2 — The "Sane Smash" Trophy Position (Solo, 3 min/day) ¶ 🇺🇸 English Stand with the racket in Continental grip, ball in your non-dominant hand. Lift BOTH arms to the "trophy position" — non-dominant arm pointing at an imaginary ball, racket arm bent with head above. Hold for 10 seconds. Do 10 reps. Why this works: the trophy position is identical for the serve and the overhead. If you can hold it for the serve, you can hold it for the overhead. The drill builds body memory. Drill 3 — The "Sane Smash" from a Tossed Ball (Solo or Partner, 10 min/session) ¶ 🇺🇸 English Stand at the baseline in serve stance. Have a partner stand at the service line on the other side and TOSS the ball high to your forehand overhead position. Track, position, turn, Sane Smash. Goal: 10 Sane Smashes in a row, all landing in the correct service box (cross-court from your position). The "fall, don't swing" cue: if your racket is "swinging" through the ball, you're trying too hard. The motion is a controlled fall, not a swing. Drill 4 — The Defensive Lob Rally (With Partner, 10 min) ¶ 🇺🇸 English You and your partner start at the baseline. You feed an easy ball to your partner. Your partner hits a deep groundstroke to you. You respond with a defensive slice lob. Your partner lets it bounce, hits it back. You lob again. Goal: 5 consecutive lob exchanges without an error. Diagnostic: if your lob lands in the service box, your arc is too low or your aim is too short. Add more shoulder shrug. If your lob lands beyond the baseline, you're overhitting. Reduce the shoulder shrug and let the backswing do the work. Drill 5 — The "Lob Volley Triangle" (With Partner, 5 min) ¶ 🇺🇸 English Set up a triangle: Partner at the baseline, you at the net on the ad side, cones (or just imagination) marking the deuce corner of the service box. Partner feeds you a ball aimed at your feet or at the body. You hit a lob volley to the deuce corner. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides. The "high contact" check: if your lob volley is going into the net, you're catching the ball too low. Let it rise to your shoulder. The lob volley needs HIGH contact, not LOW contact. 🧠 Master Cue List ¶ Cue Signal When Applies to "Scratch your back" Racket head UP, elbow bent, like scratching your back with the racket Setup, before the lob Defensive lob "Shoulder shrug" Shrug the hitting shoulder UP toward the ear at contact Contact Defensive lob "Aim deep, into the corner" The lob should land within 3 feet of the baseline, near the sideline Aim All lobs "Continental, always" V-to-bevel-2 grip for every lob and every overhead Grip All lobs and overheads "Trophy position" Both arms up, like the start of a serve Setup, before the overhead Overhead smash "Fall, don't swing" The racket head falls down through the ball; gravity does the work Contact Overhead smash "PUT IT DOWN" Not "SMASH" — you are placing the ball, not generating pace Mental Overhead smash "Cross-court is king" Aim cross-court unless you have a clean down-the-line opportunity Aim Overhead smash "Head still, chin level" Don't tilt your head back to look at the ball Setup Overhead smash "Let it bounce if too deep" If the lob is too high or too far back, let it bounce and hit a groundstroke Decision Overhead smash "High contact, not low" The lob volley only works when the ball is at or above shoulder height Setup Lob volley "Recover to the net" After the lob volley, get back to the net for the next shot Recovery Lob volley "70/30" 70% of your overhead weight is on the BACK leg at contact Stance Overhead smash "Breathe out" Small exhale on contact to release tension Pre-contact All lobs and overheads "Survive, then shine" The lob and overhead are first about getting the ball back; placement is secondary Mental All lobs and overheads ⚠️ The 7 Common Errors at 3.5 ¶ Error What it looks like Fix "Flat lob" Backswing is low, swing is horizontal, ball flies low and gets smashed Backswing UP, racket path low-to-high, shoulder shrug "Wrong grip on lob" Using Semi-Western or Eastern, lob flies long Continental for the defensive lob, groundstroke grip ONLY for the offensive topspin lob "Short lob" Lob lands in the service box, opponent hits an easy overhead Aim 3 feet short of the baseline, into the corner "Panicked overhead" Runs to the ball, swings hard, ball flies long or into the net Sane Smash: track, position, turn, fall. Grip 3-4/10, swing 30% "Craning the neck" Head tilts back to look at the ball, body off-balance Head still, eyes on the ball, chin level. Let the ball come DOWN to you "Hitting behind the body" Trying to smash a ball that's behind you, instead of letting it bounce If the lob is too deep, LET IT BOUNCE. A 3.5 groundstroke is better than a 50+ overstretched smash "Lob volley from a low contact" Trying to lob volley a ball at the waist — goes into the net Lob volley ONLY from high contact (shoulder height or above). If low, hit a normal volley or half-volley 🩺 The 50+ Reality Check ¶ Issue At 50+ the risk is... The lob/overhead-friendly answer Shoulder strain on overhead Cranking the shoulder on a high ball, rotator cuff irritation Sane Smash uses gravity, not muscle. Grip 3-4/10. Reach but don't crank. Neck strain on overhead Craning backward to look at a high ball Head still, eyes tracking the ball. Let it come DOWN to you. If too high, let it bounce. Knee strain on lob recovery Sprinting back to position for the next shot after a lob Use the "small step" recovery. Lob buys you time, use it to walk back, not sprint back. Back strain on overhead Hyperextending the lower back to reach a high ball Bend the knees, not the back. Trophy position uses knee bend + hip hinge, not back arch. Wrist/elbow on the offensive lob Brushing too hard on the topspin lob Skip the offensive lob entirely at 50+. The defensive slice lob does the same job with zero strain. Loss of confidence on high balls Fear of the overhead leads to weak, floating "moon" returns Sane Smash drill (Drill 3) builds confidence. 10 Sane Smashes in a row = brain rewires. Playing horizontal tennis only Never using the vertical game, points decided by groundstroke exchanges Lead with the defensive lob. Practice once per session. Within a month, lob will be a reflex. 🩺 The single most important 50+ rule for lobs and overheads You are not trying to win the point with the lob or the overhead. You are trying to NOT LOSE the point. A defensive lob that lands deep, even if the opponent retrieves it, gives you time to recover. A Sane Smash that lands in the correct service box, even if the opponent gets it back, puts you in attack position. Survival first, placement second, pace last. Always.** 🧘 The Tai Chi Meditation ¶ | Principle | Vietnamese | Lob|---|---|---| | Hư - Thực | A lob creates hư (emptiness) behind the opponent. An overhead exploits a real thực (substantial) high ball. Together: you create space, then you fill it. | | Bước cung | The overhead stance is a literal bow stance — front foot at 45°, back foot parallel, weight loaded. Same as tai chi's Cung Bộ . | | Lực tĩnh | A good lob is quiet power — minimum racket speed, maximum arc. A good overhead is the same — minimum effort, maximum placement. Neither shot is a "swing hard" shot. | | Cuộn lại | The defensive lob is a Lã Kình move — you yield to the opponent's pressure and redirect it UP and OVER their head. | | Luôn lỏng | Sane Smash: relaxed grip, relaxed shoulder. The racket falls, not the arm. | | Bước rơi | The Sane Smash uses Tụ Bộ — the body weight drops into the shot, not the arm swinging. The body drops, the ball drops. | 📄 Mental Checklist Before Each Vertical Shot ¶ BEFORE THE LOB: ☐ Continental grip (V to non-dom shoulder) ☐ Open or semi-open stance ☐ High backswing ("scratch your back") ☐ Aim deep, into the corner ☐ Shoulder shrug at contact ☐ Breathe out BEFORE THE OVERHEAD: ☐ Track the lob from the moment it leaves the opponent's racket ☐ Side-shuffle into position (ball 1-2 feet in front of lead foot) ☐ Turn into serve-ready stance (non-dom shoulder toward the ball) ☐ Trophy position: both arms UP ☐ Head still, chin level ☐ Grip 3-4/10 (Sane Smash = relaxed) ☐ Cross-court aim ☐ "Fall, don't swing" ☐ Finish over the non-dominant shoulder BEFORE THE LOB VOLLEY: ☐ Continental grip ☐ High contact (at or above shoulder) ☐ Open racket face (almost vertical) ☐ Non-dominant hand reaches UP ☐ Aim deep ☐ Recover to the net after the shot 📄 One-Page Printable Cheat Sheet ¶ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎾 LOB & OVERHEAD — 1-PAGE CHEAT SHEET | 4 TÌNH HUỐNG DỌC ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. Under pressure at baseline, opponent at net → DEFENSIVE LOB (slice) — Continental, high backswing, deep aim 2. At baseline, want to attack against a weak loopy ball → OFFENSIVE LOB (topspin) — Reference / for the brave 3. Opponent hits a high ball (lob, moonball, floater) → SANE SMASH — track, position, turn, fall 4. You're at the net and can't pass → LOB VOLLEY — high contact, deep aim, recover to net / OR COUNTER-OVERHEAD if time ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── THE DEFENSIVE LOB | LOB PHÒNG THỦ ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── • Grip: Continental (V → non-dom shoulder) • Stance: Open or semi-open • Backswing: HIGH ("scratch your back") • Contact: Front of body, chest-to-shoulder height • Racket face: Slightly open (Continental does this) • Swing path: Low to high (vertical, not horizontal) • Shoulder shrug: Yes — adds 6-12 inches of arc • Aim: 3 feet inside the baseline, into the corner • Sound: "phập" = clean (good) | "bộp" = flat (bad) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── THE SANE SMASH | LOB VOLLEY ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── • Grip: Continental • Contact: HIGH (at or above shoulder — not lower) • Racket face: Open, almost vertical • Non-dom hand: Reaches UP to track and balance • Aim: Deep, into the corner (same as groundstroke lob) • Recovery: BACK to the net, do not retreat ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── THE 50+ RULES | QUY TẮC 50+ ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── • Sane Smash: Gravity does the work. No muscle needed. • Lob at 50+: The insurance policy. No shoulder load, no sprint. • High balls: Let it bounce if you have to crane your neck. • If lob is too deep: Let it bounce. Groundstroke > overstretched smash. • 70/30 weight: On BACK leg at overhead contact (loaded stance) • Survival first: Then placement. Then pace. Always. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── THE 5 CUES TO REMEMBER | 5 CÂU NHẮC NHỚ ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. "Scratch your back" — high backswing = high arc 2. "Fall, don't swing" — Sane Smash = gravity, not muscle 3. "PUT IT DOWN" — placement > pace on overhead 4. "Aim deep, into the corner" — lob's only target 5. "Survive, then shine" — don't try to win the point, don't lose it ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ THE MASTER CUE: "Lob mua thời gian. Overhead đổi thời gian thành điểm. The lob buys you time. The overhead cashes it in." ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🏁 END OF DEEP DIVE ¶ The lob and the overhead are not two separate shots. They are two answers to the same problem: the ball is in the air. Once you see them as a pair, you start playing the vertical game — and the vertical game is what decides points at 3.5.

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Watch any point at your club that ends in 4 shots or fewer. Watch the rally. Watch the geometry. The shot that ENDS the point is almost never a flat cross-court groundstroke. It's almost always a shot that went up or down — a high lob that the opponent can't reach, or a smash that the opponent can only block. Recreational tennis is dominated by the horizontal game — cross-court, down-the-line, angled. But the vertical game — high balls, lobs, smashes — is what decides points, especially when opponents are skilled enough to retrieve everything from side to side. This deep dive is about the vertical game. Two shots: the lob (you hit it up) and the overhead (they hit it up, you put it down). 🧠 Mental model Imagine a chess board. Horizontal moves (left-right) gain space. Vertical moves (forward-back, up-down) change the rules of the game . A lob doesn't just put the ball in the corner — it tells the opponent: you must hit the next shot from below your shoelaces, with your head looking up, while standing still or moving backward. That's a fundamentally different problem from "return a flat ball while balanced at net." That's why lobs and overheads decide points.

docs.text: Most 3.5 players think of the lob and the overhead as separate strokes. They're not — they're paired answers to the same problem : the ball is high (or the opponent is at the net). Here is the entire decision tree: Situation English The shot Why it works 1. You are at the baseline, opponent is at the net, you are under pressure 🇺🇸 Defensive Lob (slice) The ball goes over their head, deep, into the corner. You buy time to recover. 2. You are at the baseline, opponent is at the baseline, you want to attack 🇺🇸 Offensive Lob (topspin) Topspin lob dips back down inside the court. Opponent has to hit a high ball on the run. 3. Opponent hits a high ball to you (a lob, a moonball, a floater) 🇺🇸 **Overhead ** 🇻🇳 **Overhead ** The ball is already in the air. You finish the point. 4. You are at the net, opponent lobs over you 🇻🇳 Lob Volley (nếu không kịp lùi) The lob volley is your emergency parachute. The overhead is your finishing move. ⚠️ The 3.5 trap Most 3.5 players only ever practice Situation 4's lob volley (defensive) and never practice Situation 1 (defensive lob) or Situation 3 (overhead). They panic on every high ball. They hit a weak "moon" lob when they should be hitting a deep slice lob. They flail at overheads. The whole point of this deep dive: practice all 4 situations, starting with the defensive lob and the controlled overhead.**

Together they form the hư-thực cycle: you create space, then you fill it. Bước cung The overhead stance is a literal bow stance — front foot forward, back foot anchored, weight loaded. Same as tai chi's Cung Bộ . Lực tĩnh A good lob is quiet power — minimum racket speed, maximum arc. A good overhead is the same — minimum effort, maximum placement. Neither shot is a "swing hard" shot. Cuộn lại The defensive lob is a Lã Kình move — you yield to your opponent's pressure and redirect it upward and over their head. 🩺 The 50+ framing The lob and the overhead are the two most longevity-friendly shots in tennis. The lob is a slow, low-impact motion (no shoulder load, no violent rotation). The overhead uses gravity as the engine — you don't need to swing hard; you just need to point the racket at the ball. Both shots save your joints compared to a baseline rally.** That's why we'll lead with them in this deep dive.

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English The lob is the most under-appreciated shot in 3.5 tennis. Not because it's flashy — because it works . A 50+ player who can hit a deep, arcing defensive lob to the opponent's weaker corner will save more points than a 50+ player who can hit a 70 mph forehand. The lob is slow on your body, devastating on theirs, and it asks nothing of your shoulder.
docs.title: Chapter 2 — The Lob: Defensive + Offensive (The Insurance Policy)

docs.text: |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Defensive Slice Lob | 🇻🇳 High arc, deep, slow, underspin | 🇺🇸 When you're under pressure at the baseline, opponent is at the net | 🇻🇳 Continental (the volley grip) | 🇺🇸 A "rainbow" — high enough to clear the opponent's reach, deep enough to land near the baseline | | Offensive Topspin Lob | 🇻🇳 Faster, lower, dipping topspin | 🇺🇸 When you want to attack from the baseline against a baseline opponent who is hitting weak balls | 🇻🇳 Same as groundstroke (Semi-W or Eastern) | 🇺🇳 Lower arc, lands inside the court, kicks UP after the bounce | 🧠 Which is for 3.5? Lead with the defensive slice lob. The offensive topspin lob is beautiful when Federer does it, but at 3.5 it requires: (1) reading the opponent's depth, (2) loading the legs, (3) generating real racket head speed, (4) hitting a precise margin. Get all four right or the ball lands in the bottom of the net. The defensive slice lob asks: (1) Continental grip, (2) high finish, (3) aim deep. That's it.** The defensive lob is your insurance policy. The offensive lob is "for the brave."

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Grip: Continental. The same V-to-bevel-2 grip you use for the volley. This is the single most important decision. Eastern or Semi-Western will force the face open at contact, and the lob will fly long. Stance: open or semi-open. Stand with the front foot already pointed slightly toward the sideline (not straight at the net). This is different from your groundstroke stance. The open stance lets the chest rotate upward instead of "into" the ball. Backswing: short and HIGH. The racket goes back like a tennis serve's takeback — racket head UP, elbow bent, like you're about to scratch your back with the racket. The high backswing is what gives the lob its arc. A low backswing = a flat shot = an overhead for your opponent. 💡 The "scratch your back" cue Stand in your ready position. Lift the racket as if to scratch the middle of your back. That's the lob backswing. The higher the backswing, the higher the arc.** This is a good thing. Most 3.5 players hit a "moon" lob because they keep the backswing low and try to lift with the wrist. Don't lift with the wrist. Lift with the backswing.
docs.title: 🎯 Part 1 — The Setup (Grip + Stance + Backswing)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Contact point: in front of the body, slightly higher than a normal groundstroke contact. For a forehand lob, the ball should be caught at about chest-to-shoulder height. For a backhand lob, slightly lower (waist-to-chest). Racket face: slightly OPEN. The Continental grip does this naturally. The face should look like it's "holding water" — a slight cup. A flat face = a flat shot = a smash for the opponent. Swing path: low-to-high, brushing UP the back of the ball. The racket path is more vertical than a normal groundstroke. Imagine drawing a vertical line from knee to head — that's your swing path. The "shoulder shrug" cue: as you make contact, shrug the hitting shoulder UP toward your ear. This adds 6-12 inches of height to the arc — and it doesn't strain the shoulder because the motion is gentle , not violent. 🎯 The mirror check Stand in your open stance. Do the "scratch your back" backswing. Now imagine the ball is at chest height, in front of you. Sweep the racket from low (knee) to high (head), face slightly open, shoulder shrug at the top. Your racket should end ABOVE your head, almost like a mini-serve.** That's the lob. Practice the air swing 10 times. Then add a ball.
docs.title: 🎯 Part 2 — The Contact (The "Up and Over" Feeling)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Aim: deep, into the corner. The lob should land within 2-3 feet of the baseline , near the deuce or ad sideline. A lob that lands in the middle of the service box gives your opponent an easy overhead. A lob that lands in the corner forces them to either (a) run 20+ feet to retrieve it, or (b) hit a desperate, off-balance overhead. The "moon vs. rainbow" line: the minimum arc is when the ball clears the opponent's reach by about 2 feet. The maximum useful arc is when the ball JUST clears the net by 3-4 feet. Anything higher than that wastes energy and gives the opponent time to set up. Aim for the weaker side: if you know your opponent's backhand overhead is shaky, lob to their backhand. The lob's purpose is not just to clear them — it's to make them hit a difficult overhead. 🧠 The "Pass the test" mental model Before you hit the lob, ask: will this ball clear the highest part of their reach AND land within 3 feet of the baseline? If the answer to both is yes, hit it. If either is no, either add more arc (lift the shoulder more) or aim for the deeper part of the court. A lob that doesn't pass the test is a free point for the opponent.**
docs.title: 🎯 Part 3 — The Aim and Depth (Where to Land It)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English The offensive lob is the inverse of the defensive lob. Same idea (ball goes over the opponent's head), different execution. Grip: same as your groundstroke (Semi-W or Eastern). The face needs to close over the top of the ball to generate topspin. Contact: lower and more aggressive. The ball is hit at about waist height, with a brushing-up motion, brushing the back of the ball from 7 o'clock to 1 o'clock (or 5 to 11 for backhand). The topspin makes the ball dip back down inside the court. Trajectory: lower arc, lands inside. The offensive lob clears the net by only 1-2 feet and lands inside the court. The topspin makes the ball "kick up" after the bounce, which is what bothers the opponent. When to use it: against a baseline opponent who is hitting weak, loopy balls from the back of the court. The offensive lob is a counter-attack. 🇺🇸 English --- The overhead smash is the most under-shot shot in 3.5 tennis. Recreational players see a high ball, panic, run around in circles, and either shank it into the fence or float it back as a moonball. Here's the truth: the overhead is a serve that comes to you. Same grip (Continental), same contact point (racket head above the ball, fully extended), same finish (over the non-dominant shoulder). The only thing different is the ball is in the air instead of being tossed. Once you see the overhead as "a serve that already happened," the panic disappears. You have all the time in the world. You don't need to swing hard. You just need to point the racket at the ball and let gravity help.
docs.title: Offensive Topspin Lob — The Brave Shot (Reference)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Reason 1 — They don't get into position early. The ball is high, the player is at the baseline, the lob keeps rising. The player runs around, looks up, and arrives just as the ball is at its peak. You must be in position BEFORE the ball reaches its peak. That means tracking the lob from the moment it leaves your opponent's racket. Reason 2 — They look up at the sky. The moment you tilt your head back, your body starts to lean back too. The leaning-back posture takes the legs out of the shot — and legs are the engine of the overhead. Keep your head still, eyes on the ball, chin level. Reason 3 — They try to "swing" the overhead like a groundstroke. A groundstroke generates pace by swinging. An overhead generates pace by falling — the racket falls from a high position, gravity does the work. No swing needed. Just point and fall. Reason 4 — They use the wrong grip. Using Eastern or Semi-Western for the overhead puts the racket face too open at contact, and the ball flies long. Continental is mandatory — same as the serve. 🧠 The "serve that already happened" mental model Every overhead is a serve. The opponent just tossed it for you. You have all the time in the world to set up. The ball is in the air, coming down at a comfortable pace. The net is the same height. The court is the same shape. The only difference from your serve: you're not tossing, you're intercepting. Treat the overhead like a serve and your success rate will jump from 30% to 80%.**
docs.title: Why Recreational Players Miss Overheads
The Sane Smash — 3.5+ Overhead Framework

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Step 1: Side-shuffle to position. The instant your opponent makes contact with the lob, side-shuffle so the ball will land slightly IN FRONT of your lead foot. The ball's "sweet spot" is about 1-2 feet in front of the front foot. Step 2: Turn sideways to the ball. Once in position, rotate your body so the non-dominant shoulder points to the ball. You're now in a serve-ready position — same as the start of a serve. | Step 4: Free arm UP, racket arm LIFTING. Non-dominant hand points at the ball (it tracks it, like a serve toss). Racket arm lifts up, racket head above the head, elbow bent. This is the "trophy position" of the serve. | 💡 The "two-arm" cue At the trophy position of the overhead, your arms should look identical** to the trophy position of your serve. Non-dominant arm pointing at the ball (or just tossed), racket arm bent with head above. If you've ever hit a serve, you already know this position. The overhead is just the next rep.
docs.title: 🎯 Part 1 — The Tracking and Stance

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Contact: at full extension, racket head above the ball. Reach up. The contact point is the highest comfortable point of your reach. The ball is caught between the strings and gravity. Racket face: slightly closed, going down through the ball. The Continental grip naturally puts the face in the right position. The racket path goes down and through the ball — same as a serve. The ball goes down because of (a) the downward racket path, (b) gravity. The "sane smash" cue: instead of "SMASH IT," say "PUT IT DOWN." You're not generating pace — gravity is generating pace. You're just placing the ball in the court. Aim: cross-court OR down the line — both are valid. The cross-court is the safer choice (more net clearance, more margin). The down-the-line is the "winner" choice (shorter distance to the sideline). At 3.5, lead with the cross-court. Finish: over the non-dominant shoulder, racket head pointing down-and-back. Same as a serve. If your finish is over the dominant shoulder or in front of your body, your chest didn't turn. 🧠 The "downward" mental model Watch a pro hit an overhead. The racket head is at the top, the ball is below it, the racket "falls" through the ball. The ball is in the air for less than half a second. You don't have time to swing. You have time to point and let go. The "swing" is just the racket continuing its downward path after the ball has been hit. Less is more.** ⚠️ The 3.5 trap with overheads Recreational players often try to "muscle" the overhead. They grip it tight, swing hard, and the ball flies long or into the net. The Sane Smash is the opposite: grip pressure 3-4/10, swing speed 30% of a forehand, and the ball goes IN because gravity and downward angle do the work.** A controlled 50 mph overhead is a winner at 3.5. A panicked 80 mph overhead is a fault.
docs.title: 🎯 Part 2 — The Contact and Finish (The "Fall, Don't Swing")

docs.text: Situation Position of the ball The Sane Smash adjustment 1. Easy high ball (the opponent's lob is short) Ball is at or above net height, falling comfortably Standard smash. Full extension, full Sane Smash. Aim cross-court, place the ball. 2. Behind you (the opponent's lob is deep) Ball is behind your body, above your head Turn and shuffle. Side-shuffle back so the ball is in front of you. Don't try to hit an overhead with the ball behind you — that's a backhand smash, and at 3.5, the only backhand smash worth hitting is a controlled block back. Easier solution: if the lob is too deep, let it bounce. You now have a normal groundstroke. 3. Moving backward (you're running back as the lob drops) Ball is above you, you're still moving Plant, then hit. Stop your feet first, then hit. Hitting on the run is a recipe for error. The Sane Smash is a still shot, not a moving shot. 🩺 The 50+ rule for overheads At 50+, the Sane Smash is your reward for hitting good defensive lobs in your previous points. The ball comes to you, gravity does the work, your shoulder doesn't take a heavy load. The only risk is the head-still cue — your neck doesn't love craning backward. Keep your chin level, eyes tracking the ball, and let the ball come DOWN to you instead of you reaching UP for it. If the lob is so high that you have to crane your neck, let it bounce.** A 3.5-controlled forehand from the baseline is a better shot than a 50+ overstretched overhead.
docs.title: The Three Overhead Situations

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English The lob volley and the counter-overhead are the two "specialty" vertical shots that complete your toolkit. Both are situational — you won't use them every point — but when the situation calls for them, they're devastating. Both were introduced in the Volley deep dive (Ch 4). Here we expand them with the 3.5+ decision tree for when to use them.
docs.title: Chapter 4 — The Specialty Shots: Lob Volley + Counter-Overhead

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English When: you're at the net, opponent is at the net or approaching, you can't get past them. The lob volley is the "I can't pass you, so I'll go over you" shot. Grip: Continental (same as the defensive lob). Contact: HIGH, at or above shoulder height. The lob volley only works when you catch the ball high. If the ball is at your waist or lower, hit a normal volley or a half-volley — the lob volley from a low contact is a guaranteed net error. Racket face: open, almost vertical. Open the face, lift the ball. The non-dominant hand reaches UP to track the ball (and to balance the shoulders — like the tai chi "Embrace the Moon" posture from the volley deep dive). Aim: deep, into the corner. Same aim as the groundstroke defensive lob. A short lob volley is a smash for the opponent. Recovery: BACK to the net. As soon as the lob volley is in the air, recover to the net. Don't retreat. If the opponent retrieves the lob, you want to be at the net for the next shot. 🇺🇸 English --- When: you're at the net, opponent lobs over you, you have time to set up. The counter-overhead is the "I see your lob, I will put it down" shot. This is the same Sane Smash as Chapter 3 , but from a starting position at the net instead of the baseline. The mechanics are identical. The only difference: you don't have as much time (you're closer to the net, the ball has less distance to travel), so you must start tracking the lob earlier. Step 1 — As soon as the lob leaves the opponent's racket, side-shuffle BACK. Don't stand flat-footed and watch it rise. Side-shuffle back as it rises, get into position BEFORE it peaks. Step 2 — Once in position, turn into the serve-ready stance (same as the baseline overhead). Step 3 — Sane Smash as in Chapter 3. ⚠️ The 3.5 trap with the counter-overhead Many 3.5 players see the lob, panic, and run straight back without turning their body. They arrive at the ball looking up, off-balance, and hit a weak floater. The fix: track the lob, side-shuffle back, then TURN into the serve stance.** The turn is what gives you the same Sane Smash as your serve.
docs.title: 4A. The Lob Volley — Your Net Emergency Parachute

docs.text: BALL IS IN THE AIR → What's the situation? ├─ I lobbed it, opponent is running back │ └─ Did they reach it? │ ├─ YES, they hit a defensive ball → RECOVER, hit a normal groundstroke │ └─ NO, it's a winner → CONGRATULATIONS │ ├─ Opponent lobbed, I'm at the baseline │ └─ Can I get in position? │ ├─ YES → SANE SMASH (Ch 3): track, position, turn, fall │ └─ NO (lob too deep, I'm out of position) → LET IT BOUNCE, hit a normal forehand/backhand │ ├─ Opponent lobbed, I'm at the net │ └─ Can I get in position? │ ├─ YES → COUNTER-OVERHEAD (Ch 4B): shuffle back, turn, Sane Smash │ └─ NO (lob is perfect, I'm stuck at net) → LOB VOLLEY (Ch 4A): high contact, deep aim, recover to net │ └─ I'm at the baseline, opponent is at the net, I'm under pressure └─ DEFENSIVE LOB (Ch 2): Continental, high backswing, deep aim 🩺 The 50+ pattern in doubles The vertical game is the best doubles weapon for 50+ players. Why? Doubles opponents at the net are usually 8-10 feet away from you. A defensive lob is the easiest way to neutralize them — they have to hit a high overhead on the move. And your doubles partner can poach the weak reply. The pattern: my partner serves, I hit a deep defensive lob, partner poaches the reply. Three shots, one point.** This is the 50+ doubles cheat code.
docs.title: The Vertical Game Decision Tree
Chapter 5 — Drills, Cues, Warnings, 50+ Reality Check & Printable Cheat Sheet
🛠️ The 5 Drills You Can Do This Week

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Stand in your open stance, racket in Continental grip. Do the "scratch your back" backswing. Sweep the racket from low to high, face slightly open, shoulder shrugs at the top. Do 20 air swings per day, every day, for 2 weeks. Why this works: the lob backswing is the part 3.5 players skip. They go straight from "ready" to "hit." The backswing IS the shot — without it, the lob has no arc.
docs.title: Drill 1 — The "Scratch Your Back" Lob Air Swing (Solo, 2 min/day)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Stand with the racket in Continental grip, ball in your non-dominant hand. Lift BOTH arms to the "trophy position" — non-dominant arm pointing at an imaginary ball, racket arm bent with head above. Hold for 10 seconds. Do 10 reps. Why this works: the trophy position is identical for the serve and the overhead. If you can hold it for the serve, you can hold it for the overhead. The drill builds body memory.
docs.title: Drill 2 — The "Sane Smash" Trophy Position (Solo, 3 min/day)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Stand at the baseline in serve stance. Have a partner stand at the service line on the other side and TOSS the ball high to your forehand overhead position. Track, position, turn, Sane Smash. Goal: 10 Sane Smashes in a row, all landing in the correct service box (cross-court from your position). The "fall, don't swing" cue: if your racket is "swinging" through the ball, you're trying too hard. The motion is a controlled fall, not a swing.
docs.title: Drill 3 — The "Sane Smash" from a Tossed Ball (Solo or Partner, 10 min/session)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English You and your partner start at the baseline. You feed an easy ball to your partner. Your partner hits a deep groundstroke to you. You respond with a defensive slice lob. Your partner lets it bounce, hits it back. You lob again. Goal: 5 consecutive lob exchanges without an error. Diagnostic: if your lob lands in the service box, your arc is too low or your aim is too short. Add more shoulder shrug. If your lob lands beyond the baseline, you're overhitting. Reduce the shoulder shrug and let the backswing do the work.
docs.title: Drill 4 — The Defensive Lob Rally (With Partner, 10 min)

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English Set up a triangle: Partner at the baseline, you at the net on the ad side, cones (or just imagination) marking the deuce corner of the service box. Partner feeds you a ball aimed at your feet or at the body. You hit a lob volley to the deuce corner. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides. The "high contact" check: if your lob volley is going into the net, you're catching the ball too low. Let it rise to your shoulder. The lob volley needs HIGH contact, not LOW contact.
docs.title: Drill 5 — The "Lob Volley Triangle" (With Partner, 5 min)

docs.text: Cue Signal When Applies to "Scratch your back" Racket head UP, elbow bent, like scratching your back with the racket Setup, before the lob Defensive lob "Shoulder shrug" Shrug the hitting shoulder UP toward the ear at contact Contact Defensive lob "Aim deep, into the corner" The lob should land within 3 feet of the baseline, near the sideline Aim All lobs "Continental, always" V-to-bevel-2 grip for every lob and every overhead Grip All lobs and overheads "Trophy position" Both arms up, like the start of a serve Setup, before the overhead Overhead smash "Fall, don't swing" The racket head falls down through the ball; gravity does the work Contact Overhead smash "PUT IT DOWN" Not "SMASH" — you are placing the ball, not generating pace Mental Overhead smash "Cross-court is king" Aim cross-court unless you have a clean down-the-line opportunity Aim Overhead smash "Head still, chin level" Don't tilt your head back to look at the ball Setup Overhead smash "Let it bounce if too deep" If the lob is too high or too far back, let it bounce and hit a groundstroke Decision Overhead smash "High contact, not low" The lob volley only works when the ball is at or above shoulder height Setup Lob volley "Recover to the net" After the lob volley, get back to the net for the next shot Recovery Lob volley "70/30" 70% of your overhead weight is on the BACK leg at contact Stance Overhead smash "Breathe out" Small exhale on contact to release tension Pre-contact All lobs and overheads "Survive, then shine" The lob and overhead are first about getting the ball back; placement is secondary Mental All lobs and overheads
docs.title: 🧠 Master Cue List

docs.text: Error What it looks like Fix "Flat lob" Backswing is low, swing is horizontal, ball flies low and gets smashed Backswing UP, racket path low-to-high, shoulder shrug "Wrong grip on lob" Using Semi-Western or Eastern, lob flies long Continental for the defensive lob, groundstroke grip ONLY for the offensive topspin lob "Short lob" Lob lands in the service box, opponent hits an easy overhead Aim 3 feet short of the baseline, into the corner "Panicked overhead" Runs to the ball, swings hard, ball flies long or into the net Sane Smash: track, position, turn, fall. Grip 3-4/10, swing 30% "Craning the neck" Head tilts back to look at the ball, body off-balance Head still, eyes on the ball, chin level. Let the ball come DOWN to you "Hitting behind the body" Trying to smash a ball that's behind you, instead of letting it bounce If the lob is too deep, LET IT BOUNCE. A 3.5 groundstroke is better than a 50+ overstretched smash "Lob volley from a low contact" Trying to lob volley a ball at the waist — goes into the net Lob volley ONLY from high contact (shoulder height or above). If low, hit a normal volley or half-volley
docs.title: ⚠️ The 7 Common Errors at 3.5

docs.text: Issue At 50+ the risk is... The lob/overhead-friendly answer Shoulder strain on overhead Cranking the shoulder on a high ball, rotator cuff irritation Sane Smash uses gravity, not muscle. Grip 3-4/10. Reach but don't crank. Neck strain on overhead Craning backward to look at a high ball Head still, eyes tracking the ball. Let it come DOWN to you. If too high, let it bounce. Knee strain on lob recovery Sprinting back to position for the next shot after a lob Use the "small step" recovery. Lob buys you time, use it to walk back, not sprint back. Back strain on overhead Hyperextending the lower back to reach a high ball Bend the knees, not the back. Trophy position uses knee bend + hip hinge, not back arch. Wrist/elbow on the offensive lob Brushing too hard on the topspin lob Skip the offensive lob entirely at 50+. The defensive slice lob does the same job with zero strain. Loss of confidence on high balls Fear of the overhead leads to weak, floating "moon" returns Sane Smash drill (Drill 3) builds confidence. 10 Sane Smashes in a row = brain rewires. Playing horizontal tennis only Never using the vertical game, points decided by groundstroke exchanges Lead with the defensive lob. Practice once per session. Within a month, lob will be a reflex. 🩺 The single most important 50+ rule for lobs and overheads You are not trying to win the point with the lob or the overhead. You are trying to NOT LOSE the point. A defensive lob that lands deep, even if the opponent retrieves it, gives you time to recover. A Sane Smash that lands in the correct service box, even if the opponent gets it back, puts you in attack position. Survival first, placement second, pace last. Always.**
docs.title: 🩺 The 50+ Reality Check

docs.text: | Principle | Vietnamese | Lob|---|---|---| | Hư - Thực | A lob creates hư (emptiness) behind the opponent. An overhead exploits a real thực (substantial) high ball. Together: you create space, then you fill it. | | Bước cung | The overhead stance is a literal bow stance — front foot at 45°, back foot parallel, weight loaded. Same as tai chi's Cung Bộ . | | Lực tĩnh | A good lob is quiet power — minimum racket speed, maximum arc. A good overhead is the same — minimum effort, maximum placement. Neither shot is a "swing hard" shot. | | Cuộn lại | The defensive lob is a Lã Kình move — you yield to the opponent's pressure and redirect it UP and OVER their head. | | Luôn lỏng | Sane Smash: relaxed grip, relaxed shoulder. The racket falls, not the arm. | | Bước rơi | The Sane Smash uses Tụ Bộ — the body weight drops into the shot, not the arm swinging. The body drops, the ball drops. |
docs.title: 🧘 The Tai Chi Meditation

docs.text: BEFORE THE LOB: ☐ Continental grip (V to non-dom shoulder) ☐ Open or semi-open stance ☐ High backswing ("scratch your back") ☐ Aim deep, into the corner ☐ Shoulder shrug at contact ☐ Breathe out BEFORE THE OVERHEAD: ☐ Track the lob from the moment it leaves the opponent's racket ☐ Side-shuffle into position (ball 1-2 feet in front of lead foot) ☐ Turn into serve-ready stance (non-dom shoulder toward the ball) ☐ Trophy position: both arms UP ☐ Head still, chin level ☐ Grip 3-4/10 (Sane Smash = relaxed) ☐ Cross-court aim ☐ "Fall, don't swing" ☐ Finish over the non-dominant shoulder BEFORE THE LOB VOLLEY: ☐ Continental grip ☐ High contact (at or above shoulder) ☐ Open racket face (almost vertical) ☐ Non-dominant hand reaches UP ☐ Aim deep ☐ Recover to the net after the shot

docs.text: The lob and the overhead are not two separate shots. They are two answers to the same problem: the ball is in the air. Once you see them as a pair, you start playing the vertical game — and the vertical game is what decides points at 3.5.
docs.title: 🏁 END OF DEEP DIVE

docs.text: The big idea: "The Vertical Game" ¶ This deep dive frames the lob and the overhead as two answers to the same problem — the ball is in the air — rather than two separate strokes. Default = defensive slice lob + Sane Smash. Alternatives labelled "reference" or "for the brave" SYNTHESIZE | FORMAT | EN-VI side-by-side tables, the "Ladder of 4 Situations" decision tree, sound cues ("phập" vs "bộp" for slice/flat lob), printable 1-page cheat sheet (EN + VI, Surrey bag-ready) | Deep Dive | Connection to Lob & Overhead | |---|---| | Forehand (4 L-layer dives) | The offensive topspin lob is essentially a "lifted forehand" — same L1-L4 system, but with a low-to-high swing path. | | Backhand (Ch 2 — 2HB) | The backhand defensive lob is "2HB with Continental + high backswing" — same dominant-hand-drives principle, but the swing direction is up. | | Volley (Ch 4) | Lob volley + counter-overhead were introduced as Volley Ch 4 sub-variations.
